title: The b3 Sicilian
description: A powerful offbeat weapon against the Sicilian Defense, ideal to pair with the b3 French.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1np1n2/2p1p3/2B1P3/1PN.text:
Black plays a6, looking to expand on the queenside with b5.

We'll play a4, preventing Black from playing b5. This is how we want to be meeting any intended expansion with a6.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pbppp/2n2n2/2p1p3/2B1P3/1PNP.text:
Black castles their king.

We'll develop our kingside knight to e2. This is important since we want to castle and push f4.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2np1n2/2p1p3/2B1P3/1PNP.text:
Black plays d6, supporting the central pawns and opening up the light-squared bishop.

We'll castle our king.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2np1n2/2p5/2B1PQ2/1PN2N.text:
We develop our other knight to c3. With the better piece quality & activity, White certainly has a slight edge.

We can look to castle queenside and solidify our pawn structure with d3.

r1bqk2r/p3bppp/2pP4/2p3n1/8/1P3N2/PBPP2P.text:
We capture the pawn on d6. With Black's ruined structure and a great bishop on b2, White has a pleasant advantage.

If Black recaptures with the bishop, we can continue Qe2+, Nc3 and O-O-O.

And if Black recaptures with the queen, we can continue Nxg5, Qe2+ and Bxg7.

r1bqk2r/pp1pbppp/2n2n2/2p1p3/2B1P3/1PN5/.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop to e7, preparing O-O.
Black could also play d6, but it would soon transpose.

Now that our light-squared bishop has been developed, we'll play d3 and establish a solid light-squared pawn chain.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2np1n2/2p1p3/2B1PP2/1P3N.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop, preparing O-O.

We'll capture the pawn on e5.

If Black now recaptures on e5, we can capture once more with our knight.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2np1n2/2p5/2B1PQ2/1P6/PB.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop, preparing O-O.

We'll develop our kingside knight to f3.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2np4/2p1P3/2B1n3/1P3N2/P.text:
Black captures the pawn on e4.

We'll move our bishop to d5, attacking the e4 knight and threatening to double Black's c-pawns.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2np4/2pBP1n1/8/1P3N2/PBP.text:
Black moves the knight to the only safe square, g5.

We'll capture on c6, giving up the bishop pair, but doubling Black's pawns.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p2n2/2p1N3/8/1P6/PBPP2PP.text:
We capture on e5 with the knight. Material is now balanced, and, with Black's awful pawn structure on the queenside, White should have a comfortable long-term edge.

We will continue developing with O-O and Na3-Nc4.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2pp1n2/2p1p3/5P2/1P3N2/PB.text:
Black recaptures on c6.

We'll capture the pawn on e5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n2n2/2p1p3/2B1P3/1P6/.text:
Black develops the kingside knight, immediately attacking the e4-pawn.

We'll defend the e-pawn by developing our queenside knight to c3.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n5/2p1p3/2B1n3/1PN5/P.text:
Black also has the neat tactical idea Nxe4 for us to consider.

We'll capture the knight on e4.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n5/2p1p3/4B3/1P6/PBPP1P.text:
We capture the pawn on e4. The computer evaluates the position as equal - Black has the space advantage, but we have the more active pieces and a lead in development.

We can look to continue developing with Nf3 and O-O, while the immediate threat is now Bxc6+, doubling Black's c-pawns.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n5/2p1p3/4p3/1P1B4/PBPP.text: Black captures our knight, regaining the sacrificed piece.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n5/2ppp3/2B1N3/1P6/PBPP.text:
Black strikes with d5, forking our knight and bishop.

We'll retreat the bishop to d3.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2np1n2/2p1p3/2B1PP2/1P6/.text:
Black develops their kingside knight.

We'll develop our kingside knight, adding an attacker to the e5-pawn and preparing to castle kingside.

If Black now captures on f4, we should jump our knight into g5, hitting f7!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2np1n2/2p5/2B1Pp2/1P3Q2/.text:
Black develops the kingside knight.

We'll capture the pawn on f4.

Instead of ...Nf6, the scary-looking Qh4+ could easily be met with g3.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2np1n2/2pBp3/5P2/1P3N2/P.text:
Black moves the knight to the only safe square, f6.

We'll capture on c6, giving up the bishop pair, but doubling Black's pawns.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2np4/2p1p3/2B1nP2/1P3N2/.text:
Black captures the pawn on e4.

We'll move our bishop to d5, attacking the e4 knight and threatening to double Black's c-pawns.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n5/2p1p3/4P3/1P6/PBPP.text:
Black plays e5, taking central space and increasing their control over the d4 square.

Against Nc6 and e5, we'll form a light-square complex by developing our light-squared bishop to c4.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1P.text:
The main continuation is 2...Nc6. Black continues natural development and increases their control over the center.

We follow up on our previous move by fianchettoing the c1-bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2np4/2p1p3/2B1P3/1P6/PBP.text:
Black plays d6, supporting the central pawns and opening up the light-squared bishop.

We'll strike with f4, looking to break apart Black's solid central pawn formation!

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2np4/2p5/2B1Pp2/1P6/PBPP.text:
Black captures the "free" pawn on f4.

We'll move our queen out to f3, looking to recapture the pawn on f4.

r2q1b1r/pp3kpp/5n2/2p1N3/4P1b1/1P6/P1PP2.text: We capture on e5, forking Black's king & bishop and regaining our sacrificed piece. With the two extra pawns and Black's weak king, White now simply has a winning advantage.

r2q1rk1/1p2bppp/p1npbn2/2p1p3/P1B1P3/1PN.text: Black develops the bishop to e6, looking to trade light-squared bishops.

r2q1rk1/1p2bppp/p1npbn2/2p1p3/P1B1PP2/1P.text:
We expand with f4. With the dominant control over the light-squares and great attacking prospects on the kingside, White has an edge and should have a relatively easy game.

If Black ever captures our c4 bishop, we should recapture with the b-pawn.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2p1p2b/2B1P3/1P3N1P.text:
If Black captures on f3, we should simply recapture with the queen, and any Nd4 can be met with Bxd4.

Instead, Black maintains the pin by retreating the bishop to h5.

We'll attack the bishop once more with g4!

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2p1p3/2B1P1b1/1P3N2.text:
Black recaptures with the d-pawn.

We'll target the bishop with h3.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2nb1/2p1p3/2B1P1P1/1P1P.text:
We support the e-pawn with d3. White now has a comfortable advantage and promising attacking prospects on the kingside.

After Black deals with the threat on their e-pawn, we can continue to develop with Nc3 and O-O. Also, a4 is always a useful move which looks to prevent Black from expanding on the queenside (with a6 and b5).

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2nb1/2p1p3/2B1P1P1/1P3N.text: Black retreats the bishop to the only safe square.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2np1n2/2p1p3/2B1PPb1/1P3N.text:
Black develops the light-squared bishop and pins our knight.

We'll capture the pawn on e5.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/3p1n2/2p1n3/2B1P1b1/1P3N2.text:
Black recaptures with the knight. This looks natural, but is a huge mistake!

We'll capture on e5. Giving up the strong dark-squared bishop might seem odd at first glance, but there is a tactical reason behind this!

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/2p1p3/2B1P1b1/1P3N2/P.text:
Black recaptures on e5.

Boom! We'll sacrifice our bishop on f7!

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5. This is the starting position of the Sicilian Defense, which is one of the most complex openings in all of chess. 

Simply put, the move c5 introduces asymmetry into the position, and its primary purpose is to control the important d4 square.

In this course, we're going to play b3, intending a fianchetto. This is a more positional approach which aims to take our opponents into non-theoretical waters that they are probably unfamiliar with.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the b3 Sicilian! 

You can also learn this course with the b3 French, so that you're ready for any transpositions. 

Black's main response is 2...Nc6. In this chapter we'll learn how to fight it.

Let's begin with 1.e4.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/2pp1n2/2p1p3/4P3/1P1P2N1.text: We move our knight to g3. White now has a slight edge, and we'll look to continue with Nd2 and f4.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2np1n2/1Bp1p3/4P3/1P1P4.text:
Black castles their king.

We'll capture on c6, giving up the bishop pair, but doubling Black's pawns.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2np1n2/1Bp1p3/4P3/1P1P4/.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop, preparing O-O.

We'll castle our king.

r1bqkb1r/p3pp1p/2p2np1/2p1p3/8/1PN5/PBPP.text:
We move our queen to e2 and attack the e-pawn. The evaluation of this position lingers around equality, but with Black's awful structure White's chances shouldn't be underestimated.

We are bound to win the pawn back, and we'll continue to develop with Nf3 and O-O-O.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2n2np1/1Bp1p3/8/1PN5/PB.text:
Black captures on e5.

We capture on c6, giving up the bishop pair, but doubling Black's pawns.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2np1np1/1Bp5/4P3/1PN5/P.text:
Black might also look to develop in "Dragon" style with g6 and Bg7.

We'll sacrifice a pawn with e5!

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np1n2/1Bp5/4P3/1P6/PBP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight, immediately attacking the e4-pawn.

We'll defend the e-pawn by developing our queenside knight to c3.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2np1n2/1Bp1p3/4P3/1P6/PB.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and attacks the e-pawn.

We'll support the e-pawn with d3.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1P.text:
The main continuation is 2...Nc6. Black continues natural development and increases their control over the center.

We follow up on our previous move by fianchettoing the c1-bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP1P.text:
Black plays d6, supporting the c5-pawn and opening up the light-squared bishop.

Against this, we'll pin Black's knight with Bb5 and look to set up a d3/e4/f4 pawn structure. Black now has three options...

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2np4/1Bp1p3/4P3/1P6/PBPP.text:
Black might also play e5, taking central space and increasing control over the d4 square.

We'll develop our kingside knight to e2 as to keep the f4 expansion available.

r2qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2np1n2/1Bp5/4P3/1PN5/PB.text: Black unpins the knight by developing the light-squared bishop to d7.

r2qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2np1n2/1Bp5/4PP2/1PN5/P.text: We expand with f4, transposing back into the main line.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/2np4/1Bp1p3/4P3/1P1P4/P.text: Now that our light-squared bishop has been developed, we play d3 and establish a solid light-squared pawn chain. White now has a comfortable advantage, and we'll look to continue with O-O, Nc3/Nd2 and f4.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/2np4/1Bp1p3/4P3/1P6/PBP.text: Black unpins the knight by developing the light-squared bishop to d7.

r2qkbnr/pp1bpppp/2np4/1Bp5/4P3/1P6/PBPP1.text: Black unpins the knight by developing the light-squared bishop to d7.

r2qkbnr/pp1bpppp/2np4/1Bp5/4PP2/1P6/PBPP.text:
We expand with f4. The computer gives equality, but White has more space, and the position just seems easier to play for White. 
We'll continue by developing our knights (Nc3 and Nf3), and playing Qe2 and O-O-O.

To gain a better understanding of these positions, check out the game Carlsen - Ehlvest, 2018.

a6 should be met with Bxc6.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5.

Now for our 2.b3 Sicilian! 

We will fianchetto our bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
We're continuing our analysis of the b3 Sicilian with 2...Nc6.

In this study, we will be taking a look at how to respond if Black sets up with d6.

We'll open with 1.e4.

r1b1kb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/2pq4/8/1P3N2/PBPP.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

If Black takes with the pawn, we can respond with d4 and follow it up with Nc3.

We'll develop our knight to c3 and attack Black's queen.

r1bq1rk1/4bppp/p1pp4/2P1p3/4P3/1P6/PB3PP.text:
Black castles the king.

We'll capture on d6.

r1bq1rk1/5ppp/p1pb4/4p3/4P3/1P6/PB1N1PPP.text: We develop our knight to d2, looking to jump it into c4. With Black's weak queenside pawns, White now has a very comfortable edge and should have a relatively easy game.

r1bq1rk1/5ppp/p1pb4/4p3/4P3/1P6/PB3PPP/R.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop.

If Black recaptures with the queen, we should trade on d6 and enter a pleasant endgame where we will try to expose Black's weak queenside pawns.

r1bqk2r/1p1pb1pp/p1n1pp2/8/3NP3/1P6/PBP2.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop, looking to castle their king.

Not so fast! We'll move our queen out to h5 and give a check to Black's king.

r1bqk2r/1p1pb2p/p1n1ppp1/7Q/3NP3/1P6/PBP.text: Black blocks the check with g6.

r1bqk2r/1p1pb2p/p1n1pppQ/8/3NP3/1P6/PBP2.text:
We slide our queen into h6, preventing Black from castling. White is now certainly better and it's not so easy for Black to survive.

It is hard to suggest a general plan, but some common attacking ideas include Nxc6 and e5, and even the simple Qg7.

The retreating move Bf8 can simply be met with Qe3.

r1bqk2r/4bppp/p1pp4/4p3/2P1P3/1P6/PB3PPP.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop, preparing O-O.

Now we'll strike with c5, looking to sacrifice a pawn and damage Black's structure beyond repair.

r1bqkb1r/1p1p1ppp/p1n1p3/2p5/4P3/1P3N2/P.text:
Black recaptures with the knight as to not ruin their pawn structure.

We'll now castle.

r1bqkb1r/1p1p2pp/p1n1pp2/2p5/4P3/1P3N2/P.text:
Some players go for f6, looking to negate the effect of our powerful bishop on b2.

Against this, we'll immediately strike in the center with d4.

r1bqkb1r/1p1p2pp/p1n1pp2/8/3pP3/1P3N2/PB.text:
Black captures the pawn on d4.

We'll recapture with the knight.

r1bqkb1r/1p1pnppp/p1n1p3/1Bp5/4P3/1P3N2/.text:
Black attacks the bishop with a6.

We'll capture on c6 - we're giving up the bishop pair, but looking to obtain a considerable lead in development. 

Black has made a lot of pawn moves in the opening.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/2p5/4N3/1P3N2/PBP.text:
We jump our knight into e4. This move prevents Black from developing the dark-squared bishop, since it is tied down to the defense of the g7-pawn. 

White now has a comfortable advantage, and we can look to strike in the center with d4.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/2p5/8/1PN2N2/PBPP.text:
Black retreats the queen to its home square, d8.

A more active move like ...Qh5 would have run into difficulties after Na4-Nb6.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/2pp4/4P3/1P3N2/PB.text:
Black can also choose to strike immediately in the center with d5.

We'll proceed by capturing on d5.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1np4/4p3/3NP3/1P6/PBP2P.text:
Black attacks the knight with e5.

We'll capture the knight on c6.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1npp3/2p5/4P3/1P3N2/PBP.text:
Most often, Black plays d6.

Against this, we'll immediately strike in the center with d4.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1npp3/8/3pP3/1P3N2/PBP2.text:
Black captures the pawn on d4.

We'll recapture with the knight.

r1bqkb1r/5ppp/p1pp4/4p3/4P3/1P6/PBP2PPP/.text:
Black recaptures on c6.

We'll continue with c4, controlling the important d5 square.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/2pnP3/8/1P1P4/PBP.text:
We continue d3. White now has a comfortable edge - the e5-pawn is a permanent thorn in Black's side and the doubled c-pawns are a liability.

We can kick out Black's knight with c4, and continue developing with Ne2, Nd2 and O-O.

If Black tries to get rid of our e-pawn with d6, we should kick out Black's knight and follow up by supporting our e-pawn with f4.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/2pnP3/8/1P6/PBPP1.text: Black jumps the knight into d5.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP.text:
Black recaptures with the b-pawn.

We'll march forward and attack Black's knight with e5!

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/1Bp5/4P3/1P6/PB.text:
Black develops the kingside knight, immediately attacking the e4-pawn.

We'll capture on c6, giving up the bishop pair, but doubling Black's pawns.

r1bqkb1r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/1Bp5/4P3/1P6/PBP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight to e7, supporting the c6 knight.

We'll develop our kingside knight to f3, preparing O-O.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/3nN3/1P1B1N2/PB.text:
We recapture on e4 with the knight. White has the more active pieces and a considerable lead in development.

Play can develop in a handful of ways, but a common plan is Nxd4, followed by Qf3 and O-O-O.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/3np3/1PNB1N2/PB.text: Black releases the tension by capturing on e4. This is natural, but inaccurate.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/3pP3/1P1B1Q2/PB.text:
We retreat the knight to e2. The evaluation lingers around equality, but Black is the one who has to play accurately.

We will look to break with c3/b4 and castle kingside.

If Black tries to bolster the d-pawn with e5, we can look to play Qg3 and f4.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/3pP3/1PNB1Q2/PB.text: Black plays d4, attacking our knight and closing the long diagonal.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3nP3/1PNB4/PBP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight.

We'll develop our other knight, challenging the knight outpost on d4.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/4P3/1PNB1n2/PB.text:
Black captures the knight on f3.

We'll recapture with the queen.

We have a clear lead in development, and after all, Black has now moved their queen's knight three times in the opening.

r1bqkbnr/p4ppp/2p1p3/2pp4/4P3/1P1P4/PBP2.text:
We support the e-pawn with d3. There is no doubt that White is now slightly better - Black has the inferior structure and our light-squared pawn chain is negating the potential impact of Black's c8 bishop. 

We'll look to continue developing with Nd2, Nf3, Qe2 and O-O.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP.text:
Quite often, Black plays e6 on move three. By doing so, Black opens up the dark-squared bishop and is preparing a future central expansion with d5.

Black's setup is flexible but now I recommend Bb5. This is a sneaky idea with the same intentions as before: trade the bishop, play d3 and f4 etc.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/1Bp5/3nP3/1P6/PBPP.text:
Black jumps the knight into d4 and attacks the b5-bishop. This isn't super common, but it is one of the critical ways for Black to fight against the b5-bishop.

We'll retreat the bishop to d3. It looks weird - but Black can't take advantage of it.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1P.text:
The main continuation is 2...Nc6.

We'll follow up on our previous move by fianchettoing the c1- bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1Bpp4/4P3/1P6/PBPP.text:
Black immediately strikes in the center with d5.

We'll capture on c6, giving up the bishop pair, but doubling Black's pawns.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pp4/3nP3/1P1B4/PBPP.text:
Black strikes in the center with d5. Nf6 is also possible, but, as you'll see, Nf3 is a natural and good response in this circumstance.

We'll develop our queenside knight.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/p1npp3/8/2PNP3/1P6/PB3P.text:
We continue with c4. The arising pawn structure is known as the "Maróczy Bind" - White's c and e-pawns control the d5-square, making it difficult for Black to expand with ...d5. White has a slight objective edge.

We'll look to continue developing with Nc3, Qd2 and Rfe1.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/p1npp3/8/3NP3/1P6/PBP2P.text: Black supports the c6 knight by developing the bishop to d7.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5.

We'll play our 2.b3 Sicilian and fianchetto our bishop!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, we will be taking a look at how to respond if Black sets up with a quick e6 against our fianchetto idea.

We'll open with 1.e4.

r1b2rk1/p1n3pp/2p1pq2/3p4/2P5/1P4P1/P2N1.text: We develop our knight to d2. With the better structure (two pawn islands vs Black's three) and more active minor pieces, White now has a comfortable advantage.

r1b2rk1/pp1p2pp/2n1pq2/2p5/1nP5/1PN2NP1/.text:
We develop our knight to c3. White is, again, better - our pieces are more active and better placed, and Black's bishop is having an existential crisis.

We'll look to kick Black's knight away with a3 and can try to jump our knight into e4.

r1bq1rk1/p1n3pp/2p1pb2/3p4/2P5/1P4P1/PB3.text:
Black recaptures on c6 - this is of course forced, since the queen was attacked.

We'll trade dark-squared bishops on f6.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppbp/2pp2p1/2pnP3/8/1P1P1N2/P.text:
We continue with d3. Due to Black's inferior structure, White has a slight, but lasting positional edge.

We can look to continue with Nbd2.

A future Bg4 can and should be met with h3.

r1bq1rk1/pp1p2pp/2n1pb2/2p5/1nP5/1P3NP1/.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop.

We'll trade dark-squared bishops on f6.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pb1pp/2n1pp2/2p1P3/1nP5/1P3N.text:
Black opts to jump the knight into b4.

We'll capture the pawn on f6.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pb1pp/2n1pp2/2pnP3/8/1P3NP1/.text:
Black can also try to get rid of our e5-pawn with f6.

We'll attack Black's knight with c4.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pbppp/2n1p3/2pnP3/8/1P3NP1/P.text:
Black castles their king.

We will do likewise.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/1BpnP3/8/1P3N2/P.text:
Black also castles.

We'll move our rook to e1, adding some support to the e5-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1p3/2pnp3/8/1P3NP1/PB.text:
Black captures the pawn on e5.

We'll recapture on e5 with the knight.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2npp3/2pnP3/8/1P3NP1/PB.text:
The most common move here is d6. Black is looking to get rid of our dominating e-pawn.

We prefer it if Black captures on e5, so we'll simply proceed by moving our rook over to the e-file.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/4p3/2pnn3/8/1P4P1/PBPP1.text:
Black trades knights on e5.

We'll recapture with the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np2p1/1BpnP3/8/1P3N2/P.text:
Black's other option is d6, looking to immediately get rid of our e-pawn.

We'll capture on c6 and force Black to double their c-pawns.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pb2/2pnB3/3P4/1P4P1/P1P.text:
We support the bishop and expand in the center with d4. White is now comfortably better - our pieces are very active, the g2-bishop is a menace, and Black's c8 bishop won't be impressing anyone anytime soon.

If Black now captures on e5, we should recapture with the d-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pb2/2pnB3/8/1P4P1/P1PP1.text: Black moves the bishop to f6, looking to trade off our powerful dark-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppn1ppbp/2p3p1/2p1P3/8/1P1P1N2/.text:
We continue d3. Due to Black's inferior structure, White has a slight, but lasting, positional edge.

We should look to continue with Nbd2 and a4.

Any future Bg4 from Black can and should be met with h3.

r1bq1rk1/ppn3pp/2n1pb2/3p4/2PN4/1P4P1/PB.text:
Black strikes in the center with d5.

We'll capture the knight on c6.

r1bq1rk1/ppnp2pp/2n1pb2/8/2Pp4/1P3NP1/PB.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop.

We'll capture on d4 with the knight.

r1bq1rk1/ppnpb1pp/2n1pp2/2p1P3/2P5/1P3NP.text:
Most often, Black retreats the knight back to c7.

We'll expand in the center with d4!

r1bq1rk1/ppnpb1pp/2n1pp2/4P3/2Pp4/1P3NP1.text:
Black captures the pawn on d4.

Before recapturing on d4, it is important that we throw in the capture on f6.

r1bq1rk1/ppnpppbp/2n3p1/1Bp1P3/8/1P3N2/P.text:
Most often, Black voluntarily retreats the knight and attacks the b5-bishop.

Now that we've been provoked, we'll capture on c6 and force Black to double their c-pawns.

r1bqk2r/pp1pbppp/2n1p3/2pnP3/8/1P3NP1/PB.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares O-O.

We'll continue with our plan by fianchettoing the light-squared bishop.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/1BpnP3/8/1P3N2/PB.text:
Black continues with their plan and fianchettoes the f8-bishop.

We'll proceed by castling.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/2pnP3/8/1P3N2/PB.text:
Most common is e6: Black supports the d5-knight and prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop.

Against e6 we'll look to develop with g3, Bg2 and O-O.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/2pnP3/8/1P3N2/PB.text:
Black can also play g6, intending to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

Against this, we'll develop our bishop to b5, looking to eventually capture the knight and double Black's c-pawns.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and attacks the e-pawn.

We'll push forward and attack Black's knight.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n5/2pnP3/8/1P6/PBPP1P.text:
Black jumps the knight into d5.

We'll develop our knight to f3. This leaves Black with a few choices for us to examine.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np4/2pnP3/8/1P3N2/PBPP.text:
A close second in popularity is d6. Black creates tension between the central pawns and opens up the c8 bishop.

Against this, we'll develop our light-squared bishop out to b5, pinning the c6-knight and looking to double Black's c-pawns.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1P.text:
The main continuation is 2...Nc6.

We follow up on our previous move by fianchettoing the c1-bishop.

r2q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2np4/1B1n4/2PN4/1P6/PB3.text:
We attack Black's knight and expand with c4. With the more active pieces and better structure, White now has a comfortable edge.

After Black moves the knight, we'll look to capture on c6 (with the bishop) and develop our knight to c3. 

Our f1-rook will develop to e1, and our queen can often come out to f3.

r2qk2r/pp1b1ppp/2nb4/1Bpp4/8/1P3N2/PBPP1.text:
Black recaptures on d5.

We'll move our queen to e2 and give a check to Black's king.

r2qk2r/pp1b1ppp/2nbp3/1Bpn4/8/1PN2N2/PBP.text:
Black captures the pawn on d6.

We'll capture Black's knight on d5.

r2qk2r/pp1bbppp/2np4/1B1n4/3p4/1P3N2/PBP.text:
Black captures the pawn on d4.

We'll recapture with the knight.

If instead of this Black voluntarily retreats the knight to c7, attacking our b5-bishop, we can respond with c4.

r2qk2r/pp1bbppp/2np4/1Bpn4/8/1P3N2/PBPP1.text:
Black prepares to castle kingside by developing the dark-squared bishop.

At first glance, it looks like this move hangs the g7-pawn, but capturing it is simply too risky and would give Black great counterplay on the kingside.

Instead, we'll strike in the center with d4!

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2nPp3/1Bpn4/8/1P3N2/PBP.text:
Black also has the interesting option of e6, looking to recapture on d6 with the f8-bishop.

Against this, we'll develop our queenside knight to c3.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2np4/1Bpn4/8/1P3N2/PBPP.text:
Black recaptures on d6.

We'll castle our king, perhaps looking to bring a rook to the e-file.

r2qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2np4/1BpnP3/8/1P3N2/PBP.text:
Most often, Black unpins the knight by developing the c8-bishop to d7.

We'll proceed by capturing on d6.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2np4/1BpnP2b/8/1P3N1P/PB.text: Black maintains the pin by retreating the bishop to h5.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2np4/1BpnP2b/8/1PN2N1P/P.text:
We develop our knight to c3. White already has a comfortable advantage and Black is the one that has to continue accurately.

We will look to double Black's pawns with Bxc6, and g4 is always on the cards.

Castling is flexible - we can castle kingside, but Qe2 and O-O-O is also a very reasonable option.

If Black now captures on c3, we should make sure to throw in Bxc6+!

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2np4/1BpnP3/6b1/1P3N2/PB.text:
Occasionally, Black develops the bishop out to g4 and pins our knight.

We should immediately attack the bishop with h3.

Of course, if Black captures on f3, we should recapture with the queen.

r3k2r/pp1bqppp/2nb4/1Bpp4/3P4/1P3N2/PBP1.text:
We expand in the center with d4. After best play from both sides, the evaluation is close to equality, with a slight edge for White.

We'll castle queenside, and should look to capture on c5 in order to isolate Black's d-pawn.

If Black now trades queens on e2, we should recapture with the bishop.

r3k2r/pp1bqppp/2nb4/1Bpp4/8/1P3N2/PBPPQP.text: Black blocks the check with Qe7, offering a trade of queens.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5.

We'll play our b3 Sicilian and prepare to fianchetto our bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
We're concluding our analysis of the b3 Sicilian with 2...Nc6. 

In this study, we will be taking a look at how to respond if Black plays 3...Nf6.

Let's begin with 1.e4!

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/p2p1n2/1Bp5/4P3/1P1P4/.text:
Black attacks our bishop with a6.

We'll capture the knight on d7.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/3p1n2/1Bp5/4P3/1P6/PBP.text:
Black's other option is to block the check by moving the b8-knight to d7.

We'll support the e-pawn with d3.

r2q1rk1/1p1bppbp/p2p1np1/2p5/4PP2/1P1P1N.text:
We develop our queen to e2, connecting the rooks and further supporting the e4 and c4 squares.

White now has a slight edge, and we should look to continue with Nbd2.

r2q1rk1/p2nppbp/3p1np1/1pp5/4PP2/1P1P1N2.text:
We develop our queen to e2, connecting the rooks and further supporting the e4 and c4 squares. White now has a slight edge, and we should look to continue with Nbd2.

If Black expands with a5, we should meet it with a4.

Black expands on the queenside.

The alternative expansion of d5 should be met with e5!

r2q1rk1/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2p1p3/4P3/1PNP4/P.text:
We develop our queenside knight. White now has a comfortable edge, and we'll look to proceed with f4.

Any intended expansion from Black with a6 should be met with a4.

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/3p1np1/2p5/4PP2/1P1P1N2.text:
Black castles their king.

We'll do likewise.

r2qk2r/1p1bbppp/p2ppn2/2p5/4PP2/1P1P4/PB.text: Black develops the bishop to e7, preparing to castle kingside.

r2qk2r/1p1bbppp/p2ppn2/2p5/4PPP1/1P1P4/P.text:
We lash out with g4! The computer might only give White a slight edge, but Black has to play accurately in order to parry the attack that is coming their way.

Some of our attacking ideas include g5, h4 and Qf3.

r2qk2r/1p1bppbp/p2p1np1/2p5/4PP2/1P1P1N2.text:
Black fianchettoes their bishop.

We'll castle into safety.

r2qk2r/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2p1p3/4P3/1P1P4/PB.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop, preparing O-O.

We'll castle our king.

r2qk2r/pp1nbppp/3ppn2/2p5/4PP2/1P1P4/PBP.text:
Black develops the bishop to e7, preparing to castle kingside.

If Black tries d5, we should push forward with e5.

r2qk2r/pp1nbppp/3ppn2/2p5/4PPP1/1P1P4/PB.text:
We lash out with g4! The computer might only give White a slight edge, but Black has to play like a "machine" in order to parry the intimidating attack that is coming their way.

Some of our attacking ideas include g5, h4 and Qf3. Our queenside knight can also develop to c3.

r2qk2r/pp1nppbp/3p1np1/2p5/4PP2/1P1P4/PB.text:
Black fianchettoes their bishop.

We'll develop our knight to f3, preparing to castle kingside.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/p2ppn2/2p5/4PP2/1P1P4/P.text:
Black plays e6, preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop and supporting a future d5.

We'll develop our queenside knight.

r2qkb1r/1p1bpp1p/p2p1np1/2p5/4PP2/1P1P4/.text:
Black plays g6, preparing to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

We'll develop our knight to f3, preparing to castle kingside.

r2qkb1r/1p1bpppp/p2p1n2/2p5/4P3/1P1P4/PB.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop.

We'll expand with f4.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/3p1n2/2p1p3/4P3/1P1P4/P.text:
Black might also play e5, taking central space and increasing control over the d4 square.

We'll develop our kingside knight to e2 so as to keep the f4 push available.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/3ppn2/2p5/4P3/1P1P4/PBP.text:
Black plays e6, preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop and supporting a future d5.

We'll expand with f4.

r2qkb1r/pp1npp1p/3p1np1/2p5/4P3/1P1P4/PB.text:
Black plays g6, preparing to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

We'll expand with f4.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP1.text:
Black recaptures with the knight.

We'll support the e-pawn with d3.

r3k2r/pp1qbppp/2nppn2/2p5/4PP2/1P1P1N2/P.text:
Black develops the bishop to e7, preparing to castle kingside.

We'll castle our king.

r3k2r/pp1qppbp/2np1np1/2p5/4PP2/1P1P1N2/.text:
Black fianchettoes their bishop.

We'll castle our king.

r3kb1r/pp1q1ppp/2nppn2/2p5/4PP2/1P1P4/PB.text:
Black plays e6, preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop and supporting a future d5.

If an immediate d5 here, it is important that we support the e-pawn with Nbd2!

We'll develop our kingside knight to f3, preparing to castle kingside.

r3kb1r/pp1qpp1p/2np1np1/2p5/4PP2/1P1P4/P.text:
Black plays g6, preparing to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

We'll develop our kingside knight to f3, preparing to castle kingside.

r3kb1r/pp1qpppp/2np1n2/2p5/4P3/1P1P4/PBP.text:
Black develops the queenside knight. g6 is also playable, but will quickly transpose.

We'll expand with f4.

r4rk1/pp1qbppp/2nppn2/2p5/2P1PP2/1P1P1N2.text:
We expand with c4, controlling the important b5 and d5 squares. 

Similarly to the position with g6 and Bg7, the computer gives equality, but the position remains incredibly rich.

We'll look to continue with Nc3 and Qe2.

r4rk1/pp1qbppp/2nppn2/2p5/4PP2/1P1P1N2/P.text:
Black castles their king.

If Black instead strikes in the center with d5, we should look to meet it with Ne5 (see Gelashvili - Amanov, 2006).

r4rk1/pp1qppbp/2np1np1/2p5/2P1PP2/1P1P1N.text:
We expand with c4, controlling the important b5 and d5 squares. The computer gives equality, but the position is incredibly rich.

We'll look to continue with Nc3 and Qd2. To gain a better understanding of these positions, check out the game Gelashvili - Pambalos, 2018.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/3p1n2/1Bp5/4P3/1P6/PBP.text:
Most often, Black blocks the check by moving the light-squared bishop to d7.

Blocking the check with ...Nc6 would transpose back to the previous chapter.

After Bd7 we'll trade the bishops.

rn2kb1r/pp1qpppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP1.text:
Black recaptures with the queen - this is the most common.

We'll support the e-pawn with d3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP1.text:
Black develops the kingside knight, immediately attacking the e4-pawn.

Notable is that ...Nc6 would simply transpose back to the previous chapter.

We'll develop our bishop to b5 and give a check. We're going for a positional game with attacking possibilities. The key is trading off the bishop before we play d3.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5, the Sicilian Defense.

We're going to play 2.b3. This is a more positional approach which looks to take our opponents into non-theoretical waters that they are probably unfamiliar with. The main idea of b3 is to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1PP.text:
Black plays d6, supporting the c5 pawn and opening up the c8-bishop.

Often 2...d6 transposes back to other structures because Black doesn't really have any other options.

We'll follow up on our previous move by fianchettoing the c1-bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this chapter, we will be continuing our analysis of the b3 Sicilian and taking a look at how to respond if Black chooses to move their d-pawn on move two.

In this particular study, we will be taking a look at the more common of the two moves - 2...d6.

Let's open with 1.e4.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2p5/8/1PN2N2/PBPP.text:
Black develops their other knight.

We'll develop the light-squared bishop to b5, threatening to capture on c6 and double Black's c-pawns.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2p5/8/1PN5/PBPP1PPP.text:
Black develops the queenside knight.

We'll develop the light-squared bishop to b5, threatening to capture on c6 and double Black's c-pawns.

r2qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2n2n2/1Bp5/8/1PN2N2/PBP.text: Black develops the kingside knight, transposing back into the main line.

We move our queen to e2, preparing to castle queenside. The superior piece activity and lead in development secure White a comfortable edge.

As mentioned, we will play O-O-O and can look to play for Bxc6 and d2-d4.

r2qkbnr/pp1bpppp/2n5/1Bp5/8/1PN5/PBPP1PP.text:
Black develops the bishop to d7, supporting the c6 knight.

We'll develop our kingside knight to f3.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n1q3/2p5/5Pb1/1PNP4/PBP1.text: We proceed with d3. White now has a pleasant edge, and we should look to continue with Qd2 and O-O-O.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/5n2/1BpP4/8/1P6/P1PP1P.text:
Black blocks the check by developing the bishop to d7.

If Black instead blocks with the knight, we should support the d-pawn with c4.

After Bd7, we'll simply exchange bishops.

rn2kb1r/pp1q1ppp/4pn2/2pP4/2P5/1P6/P2P1P.text:
Black plays e6, looking to chip away at our central pawn wedge.

We'll respond by capturing on e6.

rn2kb1r/pp1qpppp/5n2/2pP4/8/1P6/P1PP1PPP.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

We'll defend our d-pawn with c4!

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/4qn2/2p5/2P5/1P6/P2P1PPP/.text: Black recaptures with the queen, giving a check to our king.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/4qn2/2p5/2P5/1P6/P2PQPPP/.text: We block the check with our queen. With the extra pawn, we now have a clear advantage, and should look to continue with Bb2 and Nc3.

rn2kbnr/pp2pppp/4q3/2p5/5Pb1/1PN5/P1PPB1.text:
Most often, Black responds by sliding the queen back to e6.

We'll proceed by fianchettoing the dark-squared bishop.

rn2kbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p1q3/5P2/1PN5/P1PPb1P.text:
Black captures the bishop on e2.

We'll recapture with the g-knight.

rn2kbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p1q3/6b1/1PN5/P1PPBPP.text:
Black makes use of the pin by moving the bishop out to g4.

We can't now play Nf3, because Bxf3 would shatter our pawn structure due to the pin.

Therefore, we'll attack Black's queen with f4!

rn2kbnr/ppq1pppp/8/2p5/5P2/1PN5/P1PPN1PP.text: Black retreats the queen to c7.

rn2kbnr/ppq1pppp/8/2p5/5P2/1PN5/PBPPN1PP.text:
We develop our bishop to b2. 

White now has a considerable lead in development, thanks to the time Black has spent on the queen's adventures, and we'll look to continue with d3, Qd2 and O-O-O.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p1q3/8/1PN5/P1PP1PPP.text:
Black moves the queen to e5 and gives a check to our king.

We'll block the check with our bishop. In a perfect world, we intend to follow up with Bb2, Nf3 and O-O.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pq4/8/1P6/P1PP1PPP/R.text:
Black recaptures on d5.

We'll develop our knight to c3 and attack Black's queen.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p5/8/1PN5/PBPP1PPP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight.

We'll develop our kingside knight to f3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pP4/8/1P6/P1PP1PPP.text:
Some players try to avoid losing the lead in development by attacking the pawn with 3...Nf6.

We'll quickly develop our bishop to b5 and give a check.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/8/1PN2N2/PBPP1P.text:
Black opens up the dark-squared bishop with e6.

If instead g6, we should make use of the a1-h8 diagonal by jumping our knight into e4, exploiting the pin.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/8/1PN2N2/PBPPQP.text:
We move our queen to e2, preparing to castle queenside. White simply has a very comfortable advantage and great attacking prospects with g4.

The game Bauer - Wirig, 2005. perfectly displays how quickly and easily Black might get crushed from this position.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5. This is the starting position of the Sicilian Defense. 

We'll play b3, preparing to fianchetto our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p5/8/1PN5/P1PP1PPP/R.text:
Most often, Black retreats the queen to its home square, d8.

We'll proceed by fianchettoing the dark-squared bishop, as planned.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/4P3/1P6/P1PP1PPP.text:
Every now and then, Black chooses to strike in the center with d5.

We'll proceed by capturing on d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
We're continuing our analysis of the b3 Sicilian and taking a look at how we should respond if Black chooses to play d5 on move two.

We open with 1.e4.

2kr1b1r/pp1q2pp/2n1pn2/1Bpp4/8/1P1P4/PBP.text:
We continue with d3, looking to develop our knight to d2. The position is very rich and White has a promising edge. 

Long-term, we can look to put pressure on Black's e6-pawn and make use of the weak e5 square.

r1b1kb1r/pp2qppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/8/1P3N2/PBP.text:
Black blocks the check by moving their queen to e7.

We'll jump our knight into e5, adding an attacker to Black's c6-knight!

r1b1kbnr/pp2qppp/2n5/1Bpp4/8/1P3N2/PBPP1.text: Black moves the queen to e7 and gives a check to our king. This is the only serious alternative to 6...Nf6.

r1b1kbnr/pp2qppp/2n5/2pp4/8/1P3N2/PBPPBP.text: We block the check by retreating our bishop to e2. The position is now roughly equal, and we should look to continue with O-O and d4.

r1bqk2r/pp2bp1p/2n2p2/1Bpp4/8/1P3N2/P1PP.text: We castle our king. Due to Black's ruined structure, White now has a very comfortable edge, and should look to continue with d4 and Nc3.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/8/1P3N2/PBPP.text:
Most often, Black blocks the check by moving their f8-bishop to e7.

Oops! We'll capture on f6, forcing Black to double their f-pawns.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/8/1P3N2/PBPP.text:
Black develops their kingside knight.

We'll move our queen to e2 and give a check to Black's king. Black now has three ways to block the check, and all of them have their downsides.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/1Bpp4/8/1P6/PBPP1PPP.text:
Black blocks the check by developing their queenside knight to c6.

We'll develop our kingside knight to f3.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1bn2/1Bpp4/8/1P3N2/PBPP.text:
Black blocks the check by moving their c8-bishop to e6 - this move is second in popularity.

We'll jump our knight into g5, attacking Black's bishop and threatening to win a pawn!

r3kb1r/p3qppp/2p2B2/2pp4/8/1P6/P1PPQPPP/.text:
As if the doubled pawns on the c-file weren't enough, we now give Black doubled pawns on the f-file by capturing the knight on f6! 

The arising position is very pleasant, and Black's abhorrent structure simply secures White a lasting advantage.

r3kb1r/pp1bqppp/2n2n2/1BppN3/8/1P6/PBPPQ.text:
Black develops the light-squared bishop and supports the c6-knight.

We'll capture on c6 with our bishop.

r3kb1r/pp1q1ppp/2n1bn2/1Bpp2N1/8/1P6/PBP.text:
Black supports the bishop by moving the queen to d7.

We'll capture Black's bishop on e6.

r3kb1r/pp1q2pp/2n1pn2/1Bpp4/8/1P6/PBPPQP.text:
Black recaptures with the f-pawn.

If they instead recapture with the queen, we can capture on f6 and double their f-pawns!

We'll castle our king.

r3kb1r/pp2qppp/2b2n2/2ppN3/8/1P6/PBPPQPP.text:
Black recaptures on c6.

We'll capture Black's bishop, forcing Black to double their c-pawns!

r3kbnr/pp1nqppp/8/2pp4/3P4/1P6/PBP1QPPP/.text:
We expand in the center with d4. The arising position is probably close to equality, but the computer gives White a slight edge.

If Black now trades queens, we should recapture with the knight and castle kingside on the next move.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bnppp/8/1Bpp4/8/1P6/PBPPQPPP.text: Blocking with the knight is simply too passive. Against this, we can simply proceed with natural development (as highlighted in green).

rn1qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/8/1Bpp4/8/1P6/PBPP1PPP.text:
Black can also block the check by moving the bishop to d7.

We'll move our queen to e2 and give a check to Black's king.

rn2kbnr/pp1bqppp/8/1Bpp4/8/1P6/PBPPQPPP/.text:
Black blocks the check by moving their queen to e7 (note that blocking with the bishop loses immediately to Bxg7).

We'll proceed by capturing on d7.

rnbqkbnr/1p1p1ppp/p3p3/2p5/4P3/1P4P1/PBP.text: Against 3...a6, we should look to set up with g3, Bg2, Ne2/Nf3 and O-O.

rnbqkbnr/1p1p1ppp/p3p3/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP1.text: Occasionally, Black plays a6 on move three. This early a6 is tailored to prevent us from occupying b5 at any point in the future.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1P.text:
Black plays e6 on move two. With this move, Black has opened up the dark-squared bishop and is preparing a future central expansion with d5.

We'll follow up on our previous move by fianchettoing the c1-bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5.

We'll go for 2.b3.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pp4/4P3/1P6/PBPP1PP.text:
Black follows up on their previous move, e6, by expanding in the center with d5.

Note that playing ...Nc6 here instead would transpose to Chapter 1, Study 3.

After Black's move of d5, we'll proceed by capturing the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2pp4/8/1P6/PBPP1PPP/RN.text:
Black recaptures with the e-pawn.

We develop our bishop to b5 and give a check to Black's king.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this chapter, we will be concluding our analysis of the b3 Sicilian and taking a look at how to respond if Black chooses to play e6, g6 or Nf6 on move two.

In this particular study, we will be taking a look at the most common of these three moves: 2...e6.

Let's begin with 1.e4.

r1bqkb1r/1p1n1p1p/p2p1pp1/1Bp5/4P3/1P4Q1.text:
Black attacks our bishop with a6.

We'll capture the knight on d7.

r1bqkb1r/p3pp1p/2p2np1/2p1B3/8/1P3Q2/P1P.text: We recapture on e5. With the imminent threat Qxc6+, and with the positional idea Bxf6 (further ruining Black's pawn structure), White now enjoys a slight edge.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1p1p/3p1pp1/1Bp5/4P3/1P3Q2/.text:
Black recaptures on f6.

We'll slide our queen over to g3. The queen is well placed on g3 since it pressures the d6-pawn and ties down Black's dark-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npp1p/3p1np1/1Bp5/4P3/1P3Q2/.text:
Black blocks the check by moving the b8-knight to d7 - this is the critical line!

We'll capture Black's knight on f6, forcing Black to double their f-pawns.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2n2np1/1Bp1p3/8/1P3Q2/P.text:
Black captures on e5.

We'll capture Black's knight, forcing them to double their c-pawns!

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2np1np1/1Bp5/4P3/1P3Q2/.text:
Occasionally, Black blocks the check by moving the b8-knight to c6.

We'll push forward with e5!

r2qkb1r/1p1b1p1p/p2p1pp1/2p5/4P3/1PN3Q1/.text:
We develop the queenside knight. This position is roughly equal, but requires practical tests. Black has the bishop pair, but is held back by a passive position and closed pawn structure. 

We have the d4/d5/d6 squares as a focus, with the d5 outpost for our knights and a potential pawn break (d4). We can look to continue with Nge2 and O-O.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1p1p/3p1pp1/2p5/4P3/1PN2Q2/P.text:
We develop the queenside knight. Due to Black's inferior structure, White now enjoys a slight, but long-term, positional edge.

We should look to continue developing with Nge2 and O-O.

rn1qkb1r/pp1b1p1p/3p1pp1/1Bp5/4P3/1P3Q2/.text:
Black recaptures on f6.

We'll proceed by trading bishops on d7.

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpp1p/3p1np1/1Bp5/4P3/1P3Q2/.text:
Most often, Black blocks the check by moving the light-squared bishop to d7.

We'll capture Black's knight, forcing Black to double their f-pawns!

rnb1k2r/pp1pppbp/2q3p1/1P1nP3/8/2P2N2/P4.text:
We push the b-pawn once more, and Black has no way to save the knight!

Qe6 now loses the knight to Bc4...

And Qc5 loses the knight to Ba3!

rnb1k2r/pp1pppbp/2q3p1/3nP3/1P6/2P2N2/P4.text: Black retreats the queen to c6 - still defending the d5-knight.

rnb1k2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/2qnP3/8/1PP2N2/P4PP.text:
Black captures the pawn on c5.

We'll push the b-pawn and attack Black's queen!

rnb1k2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/q1PnP3/8/1P3N2/P1P2.text:
Black tries to win the pawn back by moving the queen out to a5 and giving a check to our king, but this natural move is actually a blunder!

We'll block the check with c3.

rnbq3r/pp1ppkb1/5npp/2p5/6PP/1P3Q2/PBPP1.text:
We push h4, further supporting g5! The computer evaluates this position as slightly better for White. 

From a human standpoint, this is a difficult position to navigate as Black. Black's misplaced king, in conjunction with the raging kingside pawn storm, should give White good practical chances.

rnbq3r/pp1ppkbp/5np1/2p5/8/1P3Q2/PBPP1PP.text:
Black recaptures on f7.

We'll push forward with g4! This move threatens to win Black's pinned knight with g5.

rnbqk1nr/pp1Pp1bp/5pp1/2p5/8/1P3Q2/PBPP1.text:
We'll respond by capturing on d7. Regardless of how Black recaptures, White should be able to secure a comfortable edge with Nc3 and O-O-O.

Of course, recapturing with the bishop would simply hang the b7-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pp1bp/4Ppp1/2p5/8/1P3Q2/PBPP.text: Black blocks both threats by pushing the f-pawn one square.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p1P3/8/1P3Q2/PBPP.text:
Black retreats the knight to its home square, g8. It couldn't have gone to h5, because then g4 would trap and win it.

Now e6 both opens up an attack on the bishop and threatens checkmate!

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/4Pnp1/2p5/8/1P3Q2/PBPP1.text:
Black blocks both threats by jumping the knight back to f6.

We'll proceed by capturing on f7.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/5np1/2p5/4P3/1P3Q2/PBPP.text:
Black fianchettoes the dark-squared bishop. This is, however, slightly inaccurate.

We'll push our e-pawn and attack Black's knight!

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/2pnP3/3P4/1P3N2/P1P.text:
Black fianchettoes their bishop.

We'll capture on c5 and open up an attack on Black's knight.

rnbqk2r/ppnpppbp/6p1/2P1P3/8/1P3N2/P1P2P.text: Black retreats the knight to c7.

rnbqk2r/ppnpppbp/6p1/2P1P3/8/1P3N2/PBP2P.text:
We fianchetto the c1-bishop. White is now simply up a pawn and Black has little to no compensation for it. 
We should look to continue with Nc3, Qd2 and O-O-O.

rnbqk2r/ppnpppbp/6p1/4P3/3Q4/1PN2N2/PBP2.text: We develop our knight to c3. We now have a pleasant edge, and should look to continue with Qe3 and O-O-O.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1p1p/4p1p1/3nP1B1/3Q4/1P3N2.text:
We expose the weakened dark squares by moving our bishop to g5. White now has a very comfortable position, which the computer evaluates as borderline winning.

If Black now attacks our queen with Nc6, we should retreat it to b2.

And if Black gives a check with Qa5, we should retreat our bishop to d2.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1p1p/4p1p1/3nP3/3Q4/1P3N2/P.text: Black plays e6, defending the knight and opening up the f8-bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP1.text:
Black obstructs the diagonal by developing the kingside knight to f6.

We'll develop our queen to f3. This interesting approach activates the queen and looks to expose the potential weakness of the f7 square.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2pnP3/8/1P3N2/P1PP.text:
Black plays g6, looking to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

Instead, Nc6 would transpose to Chapter 1, Study 4.

We'll strike in the center with d4!

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/6p1/3nP3/3p4/1P3N2/P1P.text:
Black captures the pawn on d4.

We'll recapture on d4 and attack Black's knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1P.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and attacks our e-pawn.

We'll push forward and attack Black's knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/8/1P6/P1PP1PPP.text:
Black jumps the knight into d5.

We'll develop the kingside knight to f3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/2p5/4P3/1P3Q2/PB.text:
Black plays d6, supporting the c5-pawn and opening up the c8-bishop.

We'll develop our bishop to b5 and give a check to Black's king.

rnbqkb1r/ppnppp1p/6p1/4P3/3Q4/1P3N2/P1P2.text:
Black retreats the knight to c7.

We'll fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1P.text:
Black plays g6 on move two. This might not look normal considering we are first to the diagonal, but it actually scores the best for Black - so let's not underestimate it.

We'll follow up on our previous move by fianchettoing the c1-bishop. We are now threatening to capture Black's rook on h8.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5.

We'll go for 2.b3.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this final study, we will be taking a look at how to respond if Black chooses to meet our 2.b3 with either 2...g6 or 2...Nf6.

Let's begin with 1.e4!
